transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood Product), Samir Patel (NimbusApps CTO), Jordan Lee (NimbusApps Lead Eng), Maya Chen (NimbusApps Security), Terry Huang (NimbusApps PM)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary: quick hosted demo, show streaming, show params, answer latency/cost questions, clarify security and data flows.
Action items: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: alright hi everyone, thanks for taking time, this is Alex from Redwood Inference, I'm an AE, with me is Priya our SE and Carlos product, uh hi team
[00:08] Samir: hey thanks Alex, Samir here, quick note we have about 40 minutes, we'd like to see a live sandbox run and understand retry behavior, and also want to confirm we can meet our data residency needs
[00:18] Alex: yep perfect, we'll start with a quick orientation to the hosted API and console, then Priya will run a live sandbox demo showing streaming and parameter tweaks, and we'll finish with security stuff and next steps
[00:29] Jordan: cool, high level our use case is an in-app assistant with short back-and-forth conversations, sub 300ms median latency ideal, but we care about cost — we might favor smaller models if quality is good enough
[00:40] Priya: sounds good, thanks Jordan. quick housekeeping, the sandbox we'll use is rate-limited but mirrors prod behavior for streaming and retries. i'll open the playground now — one sec
[00:52] Speaker 1: (typing sounds)
[01:04] Priya: okay loading, i pasted an example chat payload. first thing — streaming: you'll see tokens arrive incrementally over a single SSE stream, that's what we call streaming; it reduces perceived latency since the client sees tokens earlier even if final generation takes longer
[01:18] Terry: question, does streaming hold any extra state on our side? like session cookies or KV cache?
[01:24] Priya: good question, streaming is just the output transport. the runtime still manages the KV cache per conversation if you enable it; that cache lives on the server side (redwood-managed for hosted) unless you run private. you can pin cache ttl or disable prefix caching if you need strict data controls
[01:39] Maya: when you say cache lives on server side — is it encrypted and is it surfaced in logs?
[01:45] Carlos: short answer: cache is encrypted at rest with KMS, and we do not persist raw user PII in audit logs; you can configure retention windows and we have an option to disable certain debugging logs. we'll follow up with the security docs
[01:58] Jordan: nice. back to streaming — can we do chunking instead? we have a websocket-based client that prefers discrete messages
[02:05] Priya: yes, you can consume via websockets or SSE and you can buffer into logical chunks client-side. the responses are the same, it's just transport. we also support callback webhooks if you want server-to-server delivery for completed outputs
[02:18] Samir: ok demo time if that's cool
[02:20] Priya: yep starting with a simple prompt: "You are an assistant that summarizes user messages in one sentence." i'll set temperature to 0.2 and max_tokens to 60. watch the stream
[02:34] [02:34] Priya: (sends request)
[02:38] [02:38] STREAM OUTPUT BEGIN
[02:38] Priya: "User asks for concise summary of meeting notes — assistant provides one-line recap with action items."
[02:44] [02:44] STREAM OUTPUT END
[02:45] Jordan: that was immediate, was it actually streaming or just small output?
[02:50] Priya: small output but still streaming. for longer outputs you'll see partial sentences come through every, say, 50-150 tokens depending on model and batch timing. the runtime tries to flush tokens frequently to reduce tail latency
[03:03] Terry: curious — how do you tune for cost? is temperature tied to cost?
[03:09] Priya: temperature affects randomness not cost. cost is primarily tokens (input + output) and the model choice/size. we recommend smaller quantized variants for high-volume assistant tasks. also prefix caching and batching help amortize cost across similar requests
[03:22] Alex: quick interjection, for your use case — if you have short back-and-forths, enabling conversation-level KV cache and a compact model often gives a good cost/latency tradeoff
[03:33] Samir: what's your recommended retry/backoff pattern if we see transient 503 or timeouts? we want to avoid duplicate messages in the app
[03:40] Priya: typical pattern: idempotency key per user-turn, exponential backoff with jitter, and use the request status endpoints to reconcile if you need strong exactly-once semantics. Redwood returns partial tokens on timeouts if the runtime was able to produce them; we document best-effort semantics — for critical flows we recommend server-side dedupe and using model-side stop tokens to mark completeness
[03:59] Jordan: can you show an example of a retry where the first attempt times out and we resume without double-processing?
[04:06] Priya: sure — i'll simulate a transient by throttling the sandbox to cause a timeout. i'll include an idempotency key in the header and then re-call. watch the IDs
[04:18] [04:18] Priya: (runs simulated request — network hiccup)
[04:28] Priya: first call returned 504 after 10s (sandbox threshold). our client then waited 1s + jitter and retried, the second call found a cached KV snapshot and continued, returning the missing tail tokens — you can avoid showing the duplicate prefix by reconciling using the last received token id or sequence number
[04:46] Samir: that makes sense. what about streaming partials — if a client disconnects mid-stream, do you keep the generation alive server-side?
[04:54] Priya: for hosted with default settings the generation continues for a short grace window and if the client reconnects with the same idempotency key you can resume; otherwise it may be GC'd. in private deployments customers can tune grace windows and longer-term retention policies
[05:10] Maya: from a security lens we need to make sure session data isn't kept longer than 24 hours — is that configurable?
[05:16] Carlos: yes retention is configurable per account and we can set a 24-hour TTL for KV and logs in the pilot. we'll include the configuration snippet in the security docs we share
[05:28] Terry: can you show the Console briefly — how we inspect per-route latency and cost?
[05:33] Alex: sure i'll switch to the console, give me a sec
[05:38] [05:38] Speaker 2: (screen share)
[05:44] Alex: here is the requests dashboard, you can filter by model, route, and time. per-route breakdown shows median/95p latency, token counts, and cost per 1k tokens. there's also a trace we can pull for a single request to see kernel selection and batching behavior
[05:58] Jordan: kernel selection? like GPU kernel?
[06:01] Carlos: yeah, that's an internal detail — the runtime picks optimized kernels based on sequence length and model profile, and you can see a label saying quant_fast or long-seq optimized. it's mostly for our internal tuning but helpful during perf debugging
[06:16] Samir: any hard guarantees on latency for hosted? we may need a 200ms p95 for short queries
[06:22] Priya: hosted has best-effort SLAs; for firm latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity and pinned model variants. hosted usually hits low latency for small models but can't guarantee a fixed 200ms p95 under heavy bursty traffic
[06:36] Jordan: what about regional routing? can we force traffic to eu-west?
[06:40] Alex: yes you can set routing policy per API key to prefer a region; we also have fallback to nearest region if capacity is full. for strict data residency we offer Private (VPC) deployments
[06:50] Maya: does hosted support customer-managed KMS?
[06:53] Carlos: hosted supports customer-managed KMS integrations for encrypting customer keys, and you can bring your own key in Dedicated or Private as well
[07:02] Terry: any competitors we should know about? we evaluated OtherCloudAI; they had simpler pricing but not the same KV features
[07:09] Alex: yep OtherCloudAI was mentioned earlier, and OpenHost; our differentiator is the production-first controls and observability for inference economics
[07:18] Samir: let's return to parameters — show me how to tune for more deterministic replies, e.g., for legal-sounding copy
[07:24] Priya: set temperature to ~0, top_p can be left at 1.0 or reduced to 0.7 for tighter sampling. also control length with max_tokens and use stop sequences to prevent run-ons. i'll demonstrate with an example: prompt: "Draft a one-paragraph legal-style summary" temp 0.0, top_p 0.7
[07:42] [07:42] Priya: (sends request)
[07:46] [07:46] STREAM OUTPUT BEGIN
[07:46] Priya: "Pursuant to the agreement, the party shall..."
[07:52] [07:52] STREAM OUTPUT END
[07:53] Jordan: looks good — do you have built-in safety filters for hallucinations or PII redaction?
[07:59] Priya: we have content safety checks and optional PII detectors that can redact or flag outputs. for high-sensitivity workloads you can enable stricter filters and human-in-the-loop review hooks
[08:11] Maya: what's in the audit logs? do they include token-level content?
[08:15] Carlos: audit logs include metadata and request hashes by default; you can choose to enable full payload logging for debugging, but it's off by default and auditable. retention configurable
[08:25] Samir: any example of how retries affect cost? if we retry often won't we pay double tokens?
[08:31] Priya: yes retries can increase tokens if the model re-generates the same output; that's why idempotency keys and partial-token reconciliation help. we also recommend short client-side timeouts and backoff so retries occur only when truly necessary
[08:46] Terry: on the SDK side, how do we do streaming in our React native app? we use websockets already
[08:52] Priya: we'll share example snippets; basically open a websocket to /v1/streams with the api key, send the chat messages and read incremental events. SDKs have helper abstractions for reconciling streaming fragments and deduping duplicates
[09:05] [09:05] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[09:10] Alex: quick recap before we dive into a short benchmark — agreed next steps are: send sandbox creds, share security docs, run perf test and meet again; any other asks?
[09:20] Samir: can you include cost estimates for 5M tokens/month with a compact model vs large one?
[09:26] Alex: yes we'll include a cost comparison sheet and a recommended profile for your workload
[09:31] Jordan: ok let's run the perf — Priya can you run a 1-min 50-concurrency chat generator against the compact model so we can see latency and error rate?
[09:38] Priya: starting now — this is simulated load using the perf harness, note sandbox throttle may create some retry noise so results are conservative
[09:48] [09:48] (perf run in progress; noise: repeating short logs)
[10:05] Priya: results: median latency 230ms, p95 420ms, error rate 2.5% (mostly induced by sandbox throttle). tokens per response avg 34. i'll capture the full CSV and upload to your CRM note
[10:22] Jordan: thanks, those numbers are promising
[10:25] Maya: security follow-up: I'll validate that the sandbox uses encrypted transit and request that we see an example KMS config; if ok we'll proceed to pilot
[10:35] Alex: great, we'll send the KMS snippet and SOC2 summary today. Priya will run the larger 100-concurrency test and share results by next Friday
[10:45] Terry: one last quick question: if we want model rollouts and canary — can you do percentage-based rollouts?
[10:51] Carlos: yes console supports canary rollouts per route with percentage traffic splits and automatic fallback rules if error > threshold. we'll include a short doc on rollouts
[11:02] Samir: perfect, thanks everyone. feel free to send invites for the pilot kickoff next week
[11:06] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up. bye
[11:10] End of meeting

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels (Speaker 1/2) where attendees interjected. Some technical nouns may be transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV cache" as "K V cache" or "kernel" as "kernal") — see security docs for canonical terms.
